displayQuote: You May Tell the Butcher's Wife That Lady Peel Has Finished

meta.title: Who really said "You May Tell the Butcher's Wife That Lady Peel Has Finished"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Beatrice Lillie printed this line in her 1972 memoir — but Walter Winchell told the story in 1931 with a different punchline. The full chronology.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You May Tell the Butcher's Wife That Lady Peel Has Finished'?
meta.ogDescription: Lillie's own 1972 autobiography gives this wording; the earliest printing, Winchell 1931, does not. What the record actually supports.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1894–1989 · Canadian-born British revue star, Lady Peel by marriage
answer.sourceLine: Lillie printed this exact sentence in her 1972 autobiography Every Other Inch a Lady, recalling a hairdressing appointment at Elizabeth Arden’s and an audible sniff from a Mrs. Armour of the Chicago meat-packing family. But the anecdote was already circulating in print in December 1931, in Walter Winchell’s column, with a different setting and a different punchline — so the wording everyone quotes rests on a first-person memory set down four decades after the story first appeared. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes an incident probably did happen and that Lillie’s own account is the single most important telling, while noting that the details vary at every retelling.

source.heading: Where the wording comes from

docMeta.dd: Doubleday & Company, Garden City, N.Y., 1972 — the passage at page 56
Walter Winchell, “On Broadway,” The Scranton Republican, 18 December 1931 — different setting, different punchline
Attributed — a first-person account written decades after the event, with no contemporaneous record of the remark

source.excerpt: A few minutes later the svelte, well-groomed star appeared. Ignoring Mrs. Armour completely, she addressed her icy parting remark to the manager: “You may tell the butcher’s wife that Lady Peele has finished.”
trail: 18 December 1931 — the first known telling, in Walter Winchell’s syndicated column: a Chicago dress-shop fitting, an unnamed “stock yard prince”’s wife, and the exit line “Tell the butcher’s wife that Lady Peel has been fitted and she may go in now,” as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗.
6 March 1935 — the modern wording surfaces in a Chapel Hill student paper ↗, now in a Chicago beauty shop, naming Mrs. Ogden Armour and spelling the title “Lady Peele.”
1944 — Bennett Cerf’s bestselling Try and Stop Me ↗ carries the story to a mass audience with a Mrs. Swift next on the appointment calendar at a Chicago modiste’s instead.
1972 — Lillie tells it herself in Every Other Inch a Lady ↗, at Elizabeth Arden’s during the run of Set to Music; the passage is at page 56, verified on paper by QI ↗.
source.excerptNote: This 1935 college-paper column — which credits the story second-hand to an “Ed Moyer” and misspells the title as “Peele” — is the earliest freely readable printing of the modern wording. Lillie’s own 1972 memoir gives the same sentence with the spelling corrected, but sets it at Elizabeth Arden’s rather than a Chicago beauty shop.

source.rightsHolder: The estate of Beatrice Lillie and Doubleday & Company, publisher of the 1972 autobiography
source.rightsNote: The wording quoted here comes from Lillie’s autobiography (Doubleday, 1972), which is in copyright. The earlier variants appear in 1930s newspaper and magazine columns whose US copyright status depends on renewal and has not been checked. A single quip may be too short to carry copyright on its own; the safe classification for this wording is in-copyright.

author.name: Beatrice Lillie
author.kicker: The true author, as far as the record goes
author.heading: Who was Beatrice Lillie?
author.metaLine: 1894–1989 · Canadian-born British comic actress and revue singer
author.bio: Beatrice Lillie was born in Toronto in 1894 and became one of the defining comic performers of the West End and Broadway revue, celebrated for a deadpan delivery that could puncture a room without raising its voice. She married Robert Peel in January 1920 and became Lady Peel in 1925, when he succeeded to the baronetcy — a title she used with visible relish, and which supplies the entire mechanism of this joke. She told the butcher’s-wife story herself in her 1972 autobiography, Every Other Inch a Lady, written with James Brough.

misattribution.heading: What keeps getting changed
misattribution.intro: The speaker is not really in dispute — almost every telling names Beatrice Lillie. What moves, from one printing to the next, is who she was aiming at, where it happened, and how the line actually ended.

items.scope: The woman in the next chair
items.why: Bennett Cerf’s million-selling 1944 collection Try and Stop Me put a woman who had “married into the Swift hierarchy” next on the appointment calendar at a Chicago modiste’s and ended the line “Tell that butcher’s wife that Lady Peel has finished now” — a different packing dynasty from the one Lillie herself named, as Quote Investigator transcribes ↗.

items.scope: The woman in the next chair
items.why: Armour is the name in Lillie’s 1972 memoir and in a 6 March 1935 newspaper column ↗ that passes the story along second-hand. The earliest printing, in 1931, names nobody at all — only “the wife of a stock yard prince.”

When The Brooklyn Daily Eagle ran the story in 1933 it withheld both names, printing the punchline as “Tell the butcher’s wife than Lady _____ is finished!” — a reminder of how freely the anecdote travelled before it settled on Lillie (QI ↗).

That is the memoir’s setting — Lillie writes only that she was playing in Set to Music at the Shubert Theatre and went to have her hair done at Elizabeth Arden’s; she names no city. Winchell’s 1931 version happens in a Chicago dress shop during a fitting, and the mid-1930s retellings move it to a Chicago beauty shop (chronology ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence quoted today is Lillie’s own, from page 56 of her 1972 autobiography. The printed record before that — traced by Quote Investigator from 1931 to 1972 ↗ — varies at every point except the joke itself.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: The joke is a class detonation compressed into fourteen words. Beatrice Lillie was Lady Peel — she married Robert Peel in January 1920 and took the title in 1925 when he succeeded to the baronetcy, per her biography ↗. The woman on the other side of the partition had a great deal more money and no title at all, because that money came out of the Chicago stockyards. Lillie does not answer the insult; she simply re-labels the insulter, in the third person, to a member of staff.

In her 1972 telling, Lillie sets the scene at Elizabeth Arden’s while she was appearing in the Noël Coward revue Set to Music, which opened on Broadway in January 1939. The difficulty is chronological rather than moral: Quote Investigator ↗ found the story already in Walter Winchell’s column on 18 December 1931, seven years earlier, set in a Chicago dress shop and ending on a different line. Either the memoir places a real remark in the wrong evening, or the tale had already been polished by the trade press before Lillie retold it as her own.
detailsBody: 1931 — Winchell: a Chicago dress-shop fitting, an unnamed “stock yard prince”’s wife, and the exit line “Tell the butcher’s wife that Lady Peel has been fitted and she may go in now.”
1933 — The Brooklyn Daily Eagle runs it with the actress anonymised entirely: “Tell the butcher’s wife than Lady _____ is finished!”
1935 — a Chapel Hill student paper names Mrs. Ogden Armour, moves it to a Chicago beauty shop, and prints the modern wording (spelling it “Lady Peele”).
1939 — Collier’s adds a coda asking the butcher’s wife to spare a flitch of bacon until the weather clears.

1944 — Bennett Cerf’s Try and Stop Me swaps Armour for Swift; 1964 — a Maryland columnist reverses it so that Lillie is the one kept waiting; 1972 — Lillie’s own version, at Elizabeth Arden’s, with Mrs. Armour restored.
context.pull: The story reached print seven years before the evening the memoir sets it on.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator investigated this quote under the heading 'Beatrice Lillie? Apocryphal?', found the earliest evidence in Walter Winchell's column of 18 December 1931 (Scranton Republican, p.5) with the wording 'Tell the butcher's wife that Lady Peel has been fitted and she may go in now', traced variants in 1933 (Brooklyn Daily Eagle), 1935 (Daily Tar Heel, Mrs. Armour, 'Lady Peele has finished'), 1939 (Collier's, flitch of bacon), 1944 (Bennett Cerf, Try and Stop Me, Mrs. Swift), 1964 (Cumberland Evening Times, reversed), and 1972 (Lillie's Every Other Inch a Lady, page 56, Doubleday, Elizabeth Arden's, Mrs. Armour, 'You may tell the butcher's wife that Lady Peel has finished'), concluding an incident probably occurred but details varied and Lillie's account came more than forty years later.

The 6 March 1935 Daily Tar Heel, page 2, prints the anecdote crediting 'Ed Moyer', names Mrs. Ogden Armour of the meat-packing concern, sets it in a Chicago beauty shop, and ends: 'You may tell the butcher's wife that Lady Peele has finished.'

Internet Archive catalog record confirms 'Every other inch a lady' by Lillie, Beatrice, 1894-1989, with Brough, James, published Garden City, N.Y., Doubleday, 1972; the scan is access-restricted (lending).

Beatrice Lillie was born 29 May 1894 in Toronto and died 20 January 1989; she married Robert Peel on 5 January 1920 and became Lady Peel in 1925 when he succeeded to the baronetcy; the Noël Coward revue Set to Music opened on Broadway in January 1939; her autobiography Every Other Inch a Lady appeared in 1972, written with James Brough.
Try and Stop Me (1944) is a bestselling anecdote collection by Bennett Cerf, illustrated by Carl Rose, which sold over a million copies in its first two years.

Quote Investigator's Beatrice Lillie category index contains exactly one entry, 'Quote Origin: You May Tell the Butcher's Wife That Lady Peel Has Finished' — the same investigation cited above; there are no other QI articles on lines credited to her.
